blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand Variables, Data Types and Vectors

Welcome to Lesson 2: Variables, Data Types and Vectors. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Variables, Data Types and Vectors”. The goal is to variables, numeric values, characters, logical values, vectors and basic type conversion.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
R is designed for data analysis and uses vectors as a core building block. A vector holds values of a common atomic type, and many operations work across the vector without an explicit loop.

blocks.question: An R condition contains NA. What should the analyst remember?
options: NA can never appear in a comparison.
A comparison involving missing data may itself return NA and needs handling.
blocks.explanation: Missing values require explicit policy; logical filtering can be affected by NA.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Missing values require explicit policy; logical filtering can be affected by NA.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Missing values require explicit policy; logical filtering can be affected by NA.

blocks.text: Indexing in R begins at 1. Logical conditions can select rows or elements, but missing values may cause a condition to return NA rather than TRUE or FALSE.

blocks.question: A numeric vector has length 3 and another has length 5. What should be verified when combining them?
options: Whether vector recycling is intended and whether the lengths align with the analysis.
Whether the chart title is bold.
Whether R starts indexing at zero.
blocks.explanation: R may recycle shorter vectors; an unintended mismatch can generate warnings or misleading output.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. R may recycle shorter vectors; an unintended mismatch can generate warnings or misleading output.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. R may recycle shorter vectors; an unintended mismatch can generate warnings or misleading output.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Check the length and type of vectors before combining them. Recycling can be useful, but an unintended length mismatch may produce warnings or misleading calculations.

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
